results.title: The AI Compute Boom Isn’t Peaking — It’s Just Getting Started | Investing.com
highlights:
## Why is Everyone Building Compute?

- Prices are still climbing — more capacity is coming online, and rental rates are going up… significantly!
- Planning for 10 gigawatts — Meta and SpaceX are scaling to hyperscaler size, and the neoclouds are adding on top.
- This feels like the start of a new cycle — not the top the market keeps hunting for.

Every week the bear case gets louder: capex is out of control, compute is about to be commoditized, the buildout has to peak. And every week the data says the opposite.

This week the two biggest sellers of merchant AI compute, Nebius and CoreWeave, reported prices still rising even as they rush to add new capacity. So we are stepping back to answer the question underneath every capex headline: why is everyone still building compute?

## 1. Prices Are Skyrocketing

The clean bear thesis was that massive GPU deployments would commoditize compute and push rental rates down. This week ran the other way: even as capacity increased, pricing climbed, and contract terms improved alongside it.

- Nebius. Mid-term deals (1–3 years) are pricing at $20–$25M per megawatt (~$4.50/hr for GB300s), with prepayments covering 50–60% of capex; sub-six-month deals clear at $40–$50M per MW, near $9/hr. Its first capacity auction cleared 15% above the highest price it had ever charged for Blackwell, and it could sell all of its 2027 capacity today, but is holding some back for better economics.
- CoreWeave. Pushed through a ~25% price increase in July, with new contracts carrying contribution margins 5–10 points higher, even as active power grew 50% sequentially to 1.5GW and contracted power reached 4.2GW. Revenue doubled to $2.58B on a $104B backlog. CEO Michael Intrator’s read: customers "are increasingly making money from their AI products and are more willing to pay."

This chart we posted yesterday: rates climbing even as supply floods in. The near-record GPU rental and memory spot prices suggest an across-the-board compute shortage. When price keeps rising while you build as fast as you physically can, that is not a glut. It is a shortage.

...

- The hyperscalers keep guiding up. Combined 2026 capex has reached ~$860B, up ~80%, on a path to ~$1.2 trillion in 2027. Amazon lifted its number to $220B and still warned it "will still not have enough capacity"; Alphabet is at $205B and guiding "significantly" higher. Goldman now models global AI investment above $1 trillion in 2026 alone.
- SpaceX and Meta are becoming hyperscalers. SpaceX’s compute revenue hit $2.6B (+247%) and turned EBITDA-positive, with management targeting closer to 10GW than 5GW by end-2027 — a ~$200B business on their own math. Meta runs near 7GW and is doubling toward 14GW. The two names bears called "sellers who’ll flood the market" are two of the largest new buyers.
- The neoclouds are adding on top. CoreWeave and Nebius aren’t just soaking up hyperscaler overflow, they’re building their own, 1.5GW active and 4.2GW contracted at CoreWeave alone, and still selling out.

The bear case says "everyone building means oversupply." The order books say everyone is building because no one can build fast enough. Even Nvidia’s $500B financing package isn’t enough. It’s going to put online about ten gigawatts, which is what we’re expected to need next year alone.

results.title: 'Nvidia Financing' Rates Reach 18% as Analyst Warns of 2008 Echoes - Seoul Economic Daily
highlights:
Simon White, a Bloomberg analyst, warned of the risks of the "GPU financialization" being pursued by Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in research titled "Nvidia's Data Center Financialization Plan Raises Oversupply Risk," published on the 13th local time. The term refers to an attempt to turn AI computing power into an investable asset.

...

On the supply side, White expressed concern that as financialization proceeds, the market's signals of oversupply may fail to come through properly. He explained that as capital flows in amid a surge in technology firms' capital expenditure (capex) and leads to excess capacity, these signals could be masked.

On the demand side, he said a crisis could be triggered by companies gradually moving away from "token-maxing" and favoring "outcome-based pricing." As firms pressure AI model operators to use fewer tokens and GPU efficiency rises, rental prices could also fall. Contrary to claims of a GPU supply shortage, some have raised the concern that GPU utilization is low in the field. According to an April report by application performance automation platform CAST AI, average GPU utilization was just 5%. That figure represents the share wasted because companies over-secure GPUs without properly sharing them or planning their use.

"Optimists often counter with 'Jevons' paradox,' but in the market, path dependency is key," White stressed. Jevons' paradox refers to the logic that as technological progress lowers costs, demand increases, with greater usage offsetting the price decline. He warned that "at some point, the AI boom driven by large language models (LLMs) will see demand for 'intelligence' itself decline, and computing costs will fall into a prolonged slump."

...

So how are GPU loans actually being made?

Ilya Kasyan, chief technology officer of American Compute, a financial solutions firm that provides GPU residual-value insurance, said on LinkedIn last month that "GPU loan rates across the industry currently reach 9% to 18%."

The most important factor in determining rates is company size. The longer the term of the contract signed by an investment-grade firm such as a Big Tech company, the lower the rate, but otherwise it can jump to as high as 18%. According to Kasyan, GPU repayment periods are typically three to five years, and borrowers' equity share ranges from 20% to 40%. The shorter the repayment period and the larger the equity share, the more favorable the rate, but startups with weak capital can be exposed to high interest.

Kasyan stressed that loan origination fees and deposits — set aside in advance to cover future principal

highlights:
But it is not yet a full-cycle stress test.

Those residual values are being seen during a period when supply remains constrained and rental pricing is unusually strong. The real test comes after a capacity-surplus cycle – when newer systems are broadly available, rental prices normalize and customers have more alternatives.

That is the key distinction at the bottom of this slide:

...

The company reported $2.6 billion of quarterly revenue, up 112%, and ended the quarter with $104.2 billion of backlog. That figure did not include more than $25 billion of additional customer commitments signed shortly after quarter-end. Management says near-term capacity is effectively sold out, with multiple buyers competing for each GPU brought online. Pricing and expected contribution margins on recent contracts are also rising.

More than half of CoreWeave’s backlog is already attached to contracts where delivery has begun, and management expects that figure to exceed two-thirds by year-end. That is important because backlog is beginning to convert into installed, revenue-producing capacity.

Nebius provides similar evidence from a different operating model.

It signed four AI-cloud deals averaging more than $1 billion each. Customer prepayments cover roughly 50% to 60% of the associated capex, and management says it could sell its entire planned 2027 capacity today if it chose to do so. Its capacity auction also cleared 15% above its previous record price, showing that scarcity – not surplus – still clearly defines the current market.

...

The recent CoreWeave and Nebius results support that delayed-reckoning scenario. Demand clearly remains strong. Pricing remains elevated. Capacity is being absorbed. And the financing market is becoming more willing to lend against contracted compute cash flows.

But more available capital does not eliminate the market risk. It postpones the clearing test we discussed last week. As more projects receive financing, more hardware gets ordered, more sites are built and more capacity eventually becomes energized. That increases the amount of infrastructure that must ultimately find productive workloads and generate sufficient cash flow.

...

In other words, the risk window becomes 2029 through 2030, rather than one specific year. That is when utilization, rental pricing, refinancing and residual values are more likely to face a genuine full-cycle test. The probability of a soft landing – or a series of rolling, segment-level corrections after 2030 – also rises modestly, in our view. 

But there is one important caution from Ben Thompson’s recent analysis. The financing cycle can turn before the operating cycle. Clusters can still be sold out and rental pricing can remain strong while lenders begin widening spreads, reducing advance rates, requiring more equity or applying larger residual-value haircuts. So even this conditional distribution assumes the new platforms remain open and willing to finance projects on attractive terms.

...

If many institutional portfolios own loans backed by the same Nvidia systems, the same customer contracts and the same utilization forecasts, the financing may look diversified while the underlying economic risk remains concentrated. The key warning signal is not lower GPU rental prices by themselves. Lower prices could expand demand and create a healthy volume cycle (Jevons paradox). 

The alarm goes off if three things happen together:

Rental prices fall; Productive utilization weakens; And financing terms tighten.

At that point, residual values get marked down, lenders reduce advance rates, borrowers need more equity and refinancing becomes harder.

highlights:
The market’s view of the GPU cloud business may be starting to change.

Michael Burry’s bearish argument was straightforward: GPUs have a short economic life of only two to three years, while hyperscalers and cloud providers depreciate them over five to six years. In that framework, depreciation is understated, profits are overstated, and the residual value of older GPUs eventually falls close to zero.

But recent evidence is moving in the opposite direction. Rental prices for older GPUs such as the A100 and H100 have been rising rather than collapsing. CoreWeave has also signed a fully priced contract for A100 capacity through 2029, even though the chip is based on an architecture launched in 2020.

This suggests that older GPUs can retain both economic value and pricing power for much longer than previously assumed. Software optimization and rapidly growing inference demand are extending the useful life of previous-generation hardware.

The implications go beyond short-term rental prices. If older GPUs can continue generating revenue through renewals, their residual value is no longer close to zero. Once the initial contract has recovered the hardware cost, future renewals can become highly profitable incremental revenue.

That supports longer economic-life assumptions, reduces the risk of a future depreciation shock, and improves the ROIC and terminal value of existing GPU fleets. The shift is particularly important for neoclouds such as CoreWeave, whose economics depend on operating and renewing multiple generations of GPUs.

results.title: Why GPU cloud prices are quietly falling — Monster Tango
highlights:
There's no single announcement — just a handful of structural shifts in the GPU cloud market that keep pushing prices down for buyers willing to look at spot pricing.

Monster Tango Future 2 min read · Updated Aug 15, 2026

Unlike most cloud pricing, GPU cloud prices rarely move via a public announcement — they move quietly, inside spot-market rate cards, and the reasons behind it are structural, not seasonal.

## New GPU Generations Push Older Capacity Down

Every time a new GPU generation (like Blackwell-class chips) starts shipping in volume, providers sitting on large fleets of the previous generation (Hopper/H100-class) have a strong incentive to keep utilization high on that older hardware rather than let it sit idle. That shows up as steeper spot discounts specifically on the previous generation, not a blanket cut across everything.

## Neoclouds Compete Directly on Spot Pricing

The rise of GPU-specialist "neoclouds" — RunPod, Lambda Labs, Vast.ai, and others — means multiple providers now compete purely on GPU rental economics, without the broader platform and compliance overhead a hyperscaler builds into its pricing. That competition shows up most visibly in the spot market, where neoclouds are actively trying to keep otherwise-idle capacity utilized.

## Committed-Use Contracts Free Up On-Demand Supply

As more enterprise AI workloads shift to longer-term reserved or committed-use contracts with hyperscalers, that pulls baseline demand away from the general on-demand and spot pools — which, all else equal, loosens pricing in exactly the pools an individual developer or small team is actually renting from.

“GPU cloud pricing doesn't move because a provider announces a discount — it moves because a new GPU generation just shipped, a neocloud needed to fill idle capacity, or an enterprise contract just shifted where the baseline demand sits.”

## What This Actually Means If You're Renting

If a training or fine-tuning job can tolerate occasional interruption — meaning it checkpoints and resumes cleanly — it's worth periodically re-checking spot pricing rather than defaulting to on-demand or a reserved instance. The spot-to-on-demand gap tends to widen specifically during the shifts described above, not shrink.

results.title: AI Compute Boom Accelerates as GPU Prices Surge Vertically
highlights:
The AI compute market has experienced a dramatic shift in pricing dynamics, with GPU rental prices rising vertically rather than declining as expected by market participants. According to Silicon Data, the price to rent a Nvidia Hopper H100 chip for an hour has risen to $2.71, up from $1.96 at the end of November, with forward rates compiled by Silicon Data curving upwards into 2027 and 2028. Tech investor Gavin Baker noted that "everyone in 2024 and 2025 thought that GPU prices would decline slowly, if you were bearish, you thought they would decline precipitously. I don't think anyone in '24 or '25 thought that the prices of old GPUs would be going vertical." One rental customer, Baseten, revealed that its cloud service provider will push up rental prices on Nvidia Blackwell B200 GPUs from $2.63 per hour to $5.10 when contracts renew in October. Even older vintage chips are appreciating, with CoreWeave signing contracts to lease Nvidia Ampere A100 chips introduced in 2020 all the way out to 2029 at attractive prices.

## Memory Shortage Emerges as Critical Bottleneck

Memory has become a critical bottleneck in the AI arms race, with Elon Musk identifying it as the "limiting factor" in infrastructure costs. As reported by multiple sources, memory demand is compounding at 200% per year, significantly outpacing supply growth of just 20% annually. Musk specifically highlighted that "if you've got demand increasing much faster than supply, then Economics 101 would suggest that the price increases. It does not decrease." High-bandwidth memory (HBM) stacked next to GPUs is essential for feeding processors with enormous volumes of data, as modern AI models contain hundreds of billions or even trillions of parameters that must be accessed at breakneck speed. The supply gap is particularly acute because nobody can simply spin up a new memory fab on short notice, creating a situation where Economics 101 would suggest that the price increases.

...

The scale of AI compute expansion is unprecedented, with hyperscalers planning combined 2026 capex of approximately $860 billion, up 80%, targeting $1.2 trillion in 2027. As reported by Investing.com India, Amazon lifted its spending to $220 billion and warned it "will still not have enough capacity," while Alphabet is at $205 billion with guidance for "significantly higher." SpaceX's compute revenue hit $2.6 billion (+247%) and turned EBITDA-positive, with management targeting closer to 10GW than 5GW by end-2027 - a $200 billion business on their own calculations. Meta runs near 7GW and is doubling toward 14GW, demonstrating that the two companies previously identified as potential market oversupppliers are now among the largest buyers.

results.title: Issue #119: NVIDIA and Wall Street give birth to a new asset class
highlights:
The biggest chipmaker alive just made itself the bank.

NVIDIA has signed memorandums of understanding with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR to build independent financing platforms designed to mobilise over $500 billion of third-party capital for AI infrastructure over time. Jensen Huang pitched it as a shift from buying chips project by project to financing AI factories as "productive infrastructure," with the money coming from the institutions rather than NVIDIA and each deal underwritten independently on its demand, utilisation and residual value. He is careful to say the $500 billion is capital the platforms are designed to mobilise, separate from NVIDIA's revenue or any single fund. His framing of the thesis is blunter: "in AI, compute is revenue."

Most of a LinkedIn essay went to getting ahead of the obvious charge, that NVIDIA is financing demand for its own chips. The defence is that the chips hold their value: CUDA keeps old silicon earning, and NVIDIA cites H100 rental rates rising from about $1.70 to $2.35 per GPU-hour between October and March. Lower down, though, NVIDIA may provide "residual-value support" for up to 25% of a given deal, so the independent capital arrives with the vendor backstopping the resale price of the very chips it sells.

Why this matters:

- The 25% backstop is the tell. NVIDIA is putting its balance sheet behind a quarter of each deal to make a depreciating asset financeable, and it is exposed the day the residual-value case cracks. American Compute's read of 77,000 sales already puts H100 residuals in single digits by year five.
- Every deal this fortnight turns on one question: who underwrites the buildout. Volta leaned on JPMorgan in Issue #118, Fermi still needs its guaranties, Riot has twenty years to fund. NVIDIA just centralised the answer.
- It is memorandums rather than money: nothing committed, no facility closed. A $500 billion target announced while its own deals are still conditional is a headline first and an asset class second.

...

The industry lined up half a trillion for compute; the bottleneck that bit this week was memory.

Surging AI-infrastructure demand has made memory the scarce input, and the makers are pressing the advantage. SK Hynix spent the week scouting US fab sites as customers demand local supply, and HBM's manufacturing complexity keeps general-purpose DRAM tight enough that one estimate has Micron's margins reaching 95% by 2027. Three firms set the price of AI memory, and the squeeze lets them hold it.

...

HBM and DRAM sit on every accelerator, a fab takes years, and the squeeze lands as cost on every GPU buyer downstream, the neoclouds included.

results.title: AI Compute Crunch Hits Ground Level as the Scarcity Story Meets Reality
highlights:
Google News surfaced a third installment in Michael Parekh’s AI compute series, but the underlying conflict extends far beyond one newsletter headline. AI companies want unprecedented computing capacity, despite power constraints, long equipment lead times, local opposition, and uncertain customer demand.

The first two installments framed the debate from opposite directions. One examined Elon Musk’s ambition to supply gigawatts of capacity quickly. The other examined a bullish argument that demand could outgrow supply and force compute prices sharply higher.

Part three brings that argument down to ground level. A data center is not an abstract block of tokens. It is a physical project that needs land, electricity, cooling, networking, memory, permits, construction crews, financing, and customers.

That distinction changes the debate. The main conflict is no longer demand versus supply on a spreadsheet. It is the AI industry’s promise of almost unlimited compute versus the physical and financial limits of delivering it.

...

The compute crunch is real, but its most important bottleneck keeps moving.

...

The AI compute crunch has moved from chip procurement into an entire infrastructure system.

During the early generative AI boom, the shortage was easy to describe. Companies wanted more Nvidia accelerators than suppliers could deliver. Securing GPUs became a competitive advantage for model developers and cloud platforms.

That description is now incomplete. Accelerators still matter, but projects increasingly collide with power availability, interconnection delays, memory supply, cooling requirements, and construction schedules.

...

The demand-side case began with a sharper claim. If frontier-lab revenue expands much faster than compute supply, the market needs a release valve. Higher prices are one possible outcome.

...

The result is a layered shortage rather than one permanent scarcity. A frontier training cluster can remain constrained while ordinary inference becomes cheaper. A region can have available land but no timely grid connection. A completed facility can still wait for networking or memory.

This is why the third installment matters. It moves the argument away from a universal compute price and toward the local conditions that decide whether planned capacity becomes usable capacity.

...

The headline describes a shortage at ground level. That phrase should be taken literally. Data centers become real through transformers, substations, transmission lines, turbines, cooling equipment, fiber routes, and permits.

Electricity is the central constraint because advanced accelerators draw power continuously under heavy workloads. The surrounding servers, networking hardware, cooling systems, and power-conversion equipment add further demand.

...

The primary conflict is not Nvidia versus custom chips. It is urgent AI demand versus the economics required to support infrastructure for years.

OpenAI and Anthropic need capacity to train models, serve users, and expand agent products. When capacity limits growth, obtaining compute quickly has strategic value beyond the ordinary cost of a server.

That urgency can support scarcity premiums in the short term. It can also encourage long-term reservations, financing partnerships, and unconventional infrastructure arrangements.

However, urgent demand is not the same as durable demand. A contract signed during a shortage does not prove that the customer will need the same capacity under the same conditions several years later.

Parekh’s demand analysis describes a bullish argument in which frontier-lab revenue grows much faster than compute supply. Under that scenario, prices rise because buyers compete for a resource that cannot expand quickly enough.

...

A tight market today does not prove permanent scarcity, and cheaper tokens do not prove that infrastructure pressure has ended.

Both sides can be true at once. Frontier training capacity can remain scarce while the cost of common model outputs declines. The market contains different workloads, delivery schedules, and performance requirements.

...

A sustained fall in frontier-compute rental rates would weaken the strongest price thesis. Repeated delays in announced facilities would weaken optimistic supply forecasts. Falling model usage would weaken the demand case.

Conversely, longer customer commitments, rising utilization, and continued shortages across several hardware generations would strengthen the scarcity argument.

highlights:
我盯着这句"部分订单"看了好几遍。他说的虽是腾讯自家的订单，但背后是个结构性信号：在供给被掐住的周期里，高端算力现货已经成了能溢价流转、还能保值的筹码——供给最紧时，二手B200的现货甚至能保值约85%。

...

最上游有两道闸。一道是先进封装。台积电的CoWoS产线2026年全年已经售罄，英伟达一家公司就锁了约六成产能——这不是年底才紧张，是年初就排到了头。另一道闸是HBM，也就是高带宽内存，AI芯片里最金贵的内存。年初HBM价格涨了50%以上，美光全年的产能已经用"包销"模式（take-or-pay，不买也得付钱）卖光。企业想从标准渠道买一颗GPU，交期是36到52周。

需求侧还在加速。据LSEG等机构测算，四大超大规模云厂2026年资本开支合计约7250亿美元，同比涨77%；按机构拆分，其中约一半（50%）直接流向GPU与自研芯片，其余是数据中心土建、电力与网络。供给焊死、需求猛冲，缺口是结构性的，不是哪个月份的周期波动。

这里得补一句边界，免得招杠。紧缺的不是"泛算力"。确实有闲置——xAI集群利用率曝出只有11%，西部一些枢纽上架率不到三成。但闲置的是中低端，真正卡训练的是HBM与CoWoS焊死的那部分高端算力：据行业渠道统计，现货流通不到5%；稀缺高端现货与锁单转售的租金，过去半年涨了40%。这是结构性错配，不是过剩，反把"硬通货"三个字精确成了"限定在高端的那部分"。

...

松动信号现在已经能看见：H100按需租金从2025年高峰的每小时4到8美元，跌到2026年中1.99到2.69美元；Cast AI统计期内企业GPU平均利用率只有5%；Gartner预测到2027年底超过40%的Agentic AI项目会栽在ROI不清上。

美国研究机构 American Compute（专做GPU残值研究的机构）在2026年6月的《GPU Residual Value Report》里直接下结论"GPU短缺已经结束，新订单交货周期回到正常"。换句话说，一旦训练需求放缓、闲置泛滥，"锁仓"的GPU完全可能从硬通货变成滞销库存——这个裂缝是真实的，不是我替正方圆场。

更深一层是三套时钟的错配。腾讯锁的是2026年的产能，但供给端不止它一家在动：国产GPU下半年开始放量、英伟达Rubin架构2027年规模上线，都在往同一个方向压低稀缺溢价。

...

当然，这套"硬通货"逻辑有个时间窗口。刘炽平在电话会上也说了，随着GPU、ASIC和国产芯片产能逐月上来，到今年底、明年腾讯就会有"充足的产能"；资本开支高峰集中在今年下半年到2027年初，之后回落。也就是说，30%的溢价不是永久属性，是供给缺口最紧这段窗口的现象。而且折旧是真实成本——这批算力会在未来一两年摊进利润表，腾讯实质是用现金流给自己买了个"在折旧大潮到来前把AI收入做起来"的窗口期。所以"硬通货"说的是当下高端算力的稀缺定价权，不是一张永久保值的纸。

...

一套是摩根士丹利的ROI测算：推理时代头部云厂的投入资本回报率能到25%-50%——GPU租赁约31%、自有模型API约46%。它的基准假设很具体：1GW数据中心、约41万颗GB300、利用率75%、租金8.5美元/小时，算下来ROIC约31%；租金在7到10美元区间波动时，ROIC落在23%到39%。
